strengths: Novel VGI module with convergence guarantees effectively addresses the problem of noisy gradients in PINN-based value learning; Figure 3 provides compelling visual evidence of improved gradient accuracy
Well-motivated continuous-time multi-agent RL problem with clear practical relevance; Figure 1 effectively demonstrates advantages over discrete-time approaches
Comprehensive experimental validation including multiple benchmarks, thorough ablations (activation functions, loss weighting, VGI necessity), and consistent improvements across 8 settings
Strong theoretical foundation with formal lemmas and proofs for HJB formulation, instantaneous advantage, and policy improvement
Convincing demonstration of robustness to time discretization (Figure 8) showing CT-MARL maintains performance across variable time intervals while DT-MARL degrades
Clear presentation with good use of visualizations, detailed algorithm description, and comprehensive hyperparameter/architecture documentation
weaknesses: Severe restriction to cooperative multi-agent settings only; cannot handle competitive or mixed-motive interactions, which significantly limits MARL applicability and generality

Scalability concerns: experiments limited to simple systems (d=4 coupled oscillator, 2D MPE, moderate MuJoCo); no computational complexity analysis or evidence of scaling beyond ~20-30 dimensional state spaces

Critical gap in model robustness analysis: no investigation of sensitivity to dynamics/reward model errors, yet method requires accurate learned models f_ψ and r_φ; VGI's dependence on imperfect model predictions not analyzed

Non-standard continuous-time benchmark variants created specifically for this paper reduce reproducibility and comparability with other work; benchmarks remain relatively simple without evaluation on contact-rich or complex continuous dynamics

Theory-practice gaps: Theorem 3.4 assumes bounded Jacobian and sufficiently small Δt—conditions never empirically verified; proof of Lemma 3.1 assumes smooth HJB solutions which fail with non-smooth rewards
Hyperparameter tuning burden: multiple loss weights (λ_term, λ_anchor, λ_g) require careful balancing; limited sensitivity analysis and no principled guidance for new domains
Baselines are from 2021 or earlier; missing comparisons to more recent continuous-time RL methods; MADDPG comparison uses discrete-time baseline rather than continuous-time alternatives
VGI module design not fully justified: one-step lookahead not motivated; circular dependency between value and gradient learning (Eq. 13) not analyzed; no exploration of multi-step variants

strengths: Addresses underexplored continuous-time multi-agent RL problem with clear motivation and well-designed motivating example
Solid mathematical framework with proofs for HJB connection, instantaneous advantage, and policy improvement lemmas
Comprehensive ablation studies examining VGI contribution, activation functions, and loss term weighting
Diverse experimental coverage across coupled oscillator, MPE, and multiple MuJoCo environments with clear improvement over continuous-time baselines
weaknesses: Limited novelty: PINNs for HJB equations not new (Shilova et al. 2024); VGI is straightforward application of Bellman backup to gradients; primarily combines existing techniques incrementally
Severe scope limitation: Restricted to cooperative MARL only, excluding competitive and mixed-motive settings common in practice; acknowledged limitation but fundamentally restricts applicability

Weak experimental evaluation: Only 3 continuous-time baselines (from 2021), limited baseline diversity, only 5 random seeds with statistical overlap, simple problem domains (linear LQR, 2D navigation, state dim ~20)

Missing critical analyses: No model error sensitivity (requires learning f_ψ and r_φ), no computational cost comparison, no scalability demonstration beyond ~20 dimensions despite curse-of-dimensionality claims
Theoretical gaps: Theorem 3.4 VGI convergence lacks error propagation analysis for imperfect learned models; anchor loss (Eq. 17) appears ad-hoc and undermines PINN formulation justification
Methodological complexity: Four loss terms with three hyperparameters requiring careful tuning (Fig. 7); limited guidance on hyperparameter selection; no training stability analysis
Incomplete evaluation design: Continuous-time variant construction via uniform time sampling still represents discretization; robustness comparison (Fig. 8) limited to one domain and one baseline

strengths: Novel application of PINNs to continuous-time MARL with theoretically grounded Value Gradient Iteration (VGI) module addressing the practical problem of noisy gradients in PINN-based value learning
Solid theoretical contributions including HJB formulation for multi-agent settings (Lemma 3.1) and convergence guarantee for VGI (Theorem 3.4)

Comprehensive experimental validation with proper ablations consistently demonstrating VGI's importance (Figs. 2-4), design choice analysis (activation functions, loss weighting), and robustness across time intervals
Clear motivation with compelling demonstration (Fig. 1) of why discrete-time methods fail under variable time intervals, well-written presentation
Rigorous experimental methodology including multiple benchmarks and analysis of architectural choices
weaknesses: Severe scope limitation restricting applicability to cooperative multi-agent settings only—cannot handle competitive or mixed-sum games, which are central to much MARL research

Questionable fairness of experimental setup: testing true continuous-time methods against discrete-time baselines on variable-interval environments specifically designed to expose discrete-time weaknesses; missing comparisons with methods that handle variable intervals
Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing PINN-HJB techniques to MARL; VGI is interesting but relatively incremental as a one-step Bellman backup in gradient space

Insufficient scalability analysis: experiments on small systems (2-4 agents, ≤29D state); PINNs' high-dimensional limitations only partially addressed; claims of 'scaling to complex dynamics' overstated

Theoretical gaps: VGI convergence proof assumes fixed small Δt but training uses uniformly sampled Δt; error propagation from learned dynamics/reward models not analyzed; no convergence guarantee for full algorithm

Model learning inadequately analyzed: separate dynamics/reward model learning introduces errors not thoroughly studied; finite difference discretization ignored; no ablation on joint end-to-end learning
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection guidance: Figure 7 shows loss weights heavily impact performance; 'anchor loss' appears ad-hoc lacking theoretical justification
Experimental limitations: only 5 random seeds; large error bars in some results; coupled oscillator limited to linear dynamics; limited baseline comparisons against contemporary methods
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; environment modifications for continuous-time variants may be non-trivial; hyperparameter selection process underdocumented

strengths: Clear motivation addressing an important gap: discrete-time RL limitations in continuous-time systems are well-articulated with compelling examples
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple environments, thorough ablations, sensitivity analyses, and comparisons with 4 continuous-time + 3 discrete-time baselines
Solid technical approach: VGI module addresses real problem of value gradient accuracy in continuous-time control, with convergence analysis (Theorem 3.4)
Well-written and clear presentation: good problem formulation (Eq. 1), logical progression, informative figures (especially coupled oscillator example)
Theoretical contributions: Lemmas 3.1-3.3 ground the approach; Theorem 3.4 establishes VGI as contraction mapping with convergence guarantees
Practical implementation details: addresses dynamics/reward models, anchor loss, finite differences recovery, multiple design considerations
weaknesses: Critical limitation to deterministic systems: severely restricts real-world applicability; noise experiments (C.3) show significant performance degradation even with moderate stochasticity (σ²=0.5)
Limited theoretical novelty: HJB formulation and PINN-based approaches well-established; VGI is essentially gradient-space Bellman backup—straightforward rather than innovative

Artificial experimental setup: 'continuous-time' environments are discrete simulators with random time-interval sampling, not genuine continuous-time systems; no real continuous-time experiments (e.g., robotics)
Insufficient scalability evidence: largest test 113-dimensional state space; no computational cost comparisons; PINNs typically require tuning and can be slow—training time not reported

Weak VGI justification: Theorem 3.4 proves convergence but doesn't explain superiority over HJB residual alone; assumes bounded Jacobian and small Δt that may not hold during learning; Figure 3 lacks quantitative error metrics
Missing key analyses: no wall-clock time comparisons, no sample efficiency analysis (episodes vs. samples), no characterization of how approximation errors propagate to policy performance
Hyperparameter complexity: requires tuning λ_anchor, λ_g with task-dependent sensitivity (Fig. 7); systematic tuning procedure missing, reproducibility concerns

Limited baseline comparisons: only 4 continuous-time baselines; discrete-time comparison somewhat unfair since those methods aren't designed for continuous-time; missing simpler baselines (e.g., small discrete steps)
Incomplete theoretical treatment: no overall algorithm convergence guarantees; Theorem 3.4's 'sufficiently small Δt' requirement vague; incompatible with variable Δt sampling during rollouts
Restricted scope: only cooperative multi-agent settings; competitive/mixed scenarios require HJI formulations (future work), limiting applicability

strengths: Well-motivated continuous-time MARL problem with clear limitations of discrete-time approaches
Mathematically rigorous framework with proofs for HJB formulation, policy improvement, and VGI convergence (Theorem 3.4)
Sensible design of VGI module that addresses real problem of PDE residuals not guaranteeing accurate gradients
Comprehensive experiments with multiple benchmarks and ablations demonstrating VGI importance
Good visualization of problem and solution (Figures 1, 3) with ground truth validation in coupled oscillator
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: VGI is incremental application of Bellman-style recursion to gradients; PINN use for HJB established in prior work
Severely restricted scope: deterministic systems only, cooperative multi-agent settings only; stochasticity experiments show dramatic degradation
Requires learning dynamics and reward models with unanalyzed error propagation; finite difference approximation called 'unstable in practice' yet used anyway
Weak empirical validation: HJBPPO baseline shows comparable performance in many tasks with improvements within noise margins; high variance in results
Unfair DTRL comparisons: discrete-time methods not designed for variable time intervals; motivating example may reflect poor tuning rather than fundamental limitations
Theorem 3.4 requires 'sufficiently small' Δt but environment-dependent threshold (~0.15 in coupled oscillator); contraction depends on bounded Jacobians unclear for neural networks
Loss function engineering concerns: performance sensitive to weight balancing (Figure 7); anchor loss appears ad-hoc without strong theoretical justification
Scalability not convincingly demonstrated: largest experiment has 6 agents and 113 dimensions; no computational cost analysis or timing comparisons
Incomplete ablations: loss term ablation shown for only one environment; no systematic study of component importance across all environments
Method has many tunable components without clear guidance on selection; environment-dependent hyperparameter choices limit reproducibility

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine gap in continuous-time multi-agent RL with practical relevance to high-frequency control systems
Novel VGI contribution: Insightful observation that PDE residuals alone don't guarantee accurate value gradients; trajectory-aligned gradient refinement is elegant and well-motivated
Solid theoretical foundation: Rigorous multi-agent HJB formulation, policy improvement theorems, and VGI convergence proof via contraction mapping analysis

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies, multiple baselines, ground-truth comparisons in coupled oscillator, robustness to time discretization, and clear gradient accuracy visualizations
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across all tested environments (8 different tasks); Figure 3 provides compelling evidence of VGI effectiveness
Reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, implementation details, and promised code release enable reproduction
Well-structured presentation: Clear motivation, logical progression from formulation to evaluation, and generally clear writing
weaknesses: Restricted to deterministic systems: Fundamentally limits applicability; Section C.3 shows significant degradation under stochastic noise (σ² ≥ 0.5); stochastic HJB extension left as future work
Restricted to cooperative games: Cannot handle competitive or mixed-motive scenarios; would require HJI formulations not addressed; significantly limits problem domains

Model-based complexity: Requires learning auxiliary dynamics and reward models; three loss terms with hyperparameters; Figure 7 shows sensitivity to weight balancing; no principled hyperparameter selection procedure provided

Missing computational analysis: No wall-clock time comparisons, computational overhead analysis, or scalability beyond dimensionality; multiple neural networks require training but efficiency gains unclear

Theoretical assumptions underdeveloped: Theorem 3.4 requires bounded Jacobian and small Δt; Figure 13 shows performance degradation for Δt > 0.15; insufficient guidance on selecting Δt or verifying contraction conditions in practice

Fairness of baseline comparisons: DTRL baselines evaluated on environments with random time intervals they weren't designed for; Figure 8 provides more balanced comparison but limited to simple setting; more extensive fixed-timestep evaluation needed

Scalability concerns: Largest experiment is 6 agents with 113 dimensions; PINNs known to struggle in high dimensions; no comparison of PINN to alternative function approximators; unclear extension to hundreds of agents/dimensions
Limited core technical novelty: Using PINNs for HJB equations is established (HJBPPO, Shilova et al. 2024); VGI is primary novelty but relatively focused contribution
Statistical rigor: Only 5 random seeds; some results lack error bars; Walker task (Figure 2) shows modest improvements with high variance; no significance testing

Insufficient analysis of VGI applicability: Shows VGI helps in multi-agent settings but doesn't explain why; doesn't explore VGI benefits for single-agent CTRL or discrete-time methods; limited analysis of gradient amplification mechanisms in coupled dynamics
